content: Administrative data on violence against women (VAW) is collected during routine service delivery and operational activities. When this data is analyzed, reported, and shared with service providers, program managers, and policymakers, it provides timely and relevant information for monitoring service usage and planning improvements in VAW-related policies, programs, and services. Additionally, equity analyses of this data can reveal which populations are being excluded from service delivery, supporting national and subnational efforts to fulfill the Sustainable Development Goals' commitment to leave no one behind. The importance of VAW administrative data was underscored during the COVID-19 pandemic. In many regions, data from telephone helplines, shelters, and police reports indicated increased demand for VAW services. This information was critical for global and local advocacy, guiding countries to incorporate measures addressing VAW in their COVID-19 response and recovery plans. While the visibility of administrative data increased during the pandemic, its utility for monitoring service use, identifying gaps, evaluating service quality, tracking outcomes, and guiding service planning remains consistently relevant. Administrative data is invaluable for developing, monitoring, and strengthening policies and programs aimed at preventing and responding to VAW. Experiences from various countries and regions demonstrate that improving the collection and use of VAW administrative data requires a multi-year commitment and dedicated resources. Leadership and expertise from institutions responsible for VAW policies and statistics, as well as commitment from sectors providing services to survivors and engaging with perpetrators, are essential for progress. Civil society experts and survivors themselves also play a crucial role and should be actively consulted and included in governance systems overseeing the development and implementation of VAW administrative data systems. The benefits of strengthening VAW administrative data collection and use extend beyond merely generating information. This process is intertwined with enhancing service providers' understanding of VAW and their responses. Training on data collection in the context of VAW service provision is critical, as it can promote non-discriminatory, empathetic communication and respect for confidentiality. The data collection process, including the design of forms, can also drive quality improvements by enabling the monitoring of implementation over time. The analysis, reporting, and communication of administrative data facilitate its use in improving VAW prevention and response. Reporting and data communication create opportunities for informed dialogue and can hold duty bearers accountable. Strengthening VAW administrative data systems lays the foundation for dialogue within governments and between government representatives and other stakeholders, such as civil society organizations, researchers, and international entities, to catalyze improvements. Regional and country experiences highlight that inter-institutional coordination and prioritization of capacity building are key to advancing VAW administrative data collection, reporting, and communication. These efforts have mobilized political will and resources not only for improving VAW administrative data systems but also for broader prevention and response initiatives addressing VAW.
